result:
There is a particular kind of attention that only exists in thresholds—the doorway where you’re neither fully inside nor outside, the moment after a question is asked but before the answer lands, the stretch of sky at 6:47 in the evening when the sun has surrendered but the world hasn’t yet committed to darkness. I’ve become somewhat obsessed with these in-between spaces, not because they’re comfortable (they rarely are) but because they’re honest. Everything else is performance: the morning rush, the polished meeting, the dinner conversation where everyone pretends they’re not tired. The threshold is where the mask slips.

I think of train stations that no longer serve as destinations but as pauses—those long underground corridors where the air smells of ozone and old coffee, where a thousand strangers share the same temporary citizenship of “in transit.” You don’t need to be going anywhere specific to belong there. The hum of electricity in the walls becomes a kind of silence, not the absence of sound but its redistribution. You become porous. Thoughts that were locked in the basement of your mind start circulating, like air through an open window.

There is also the in-between of memory. Not the sharp photograph of an event, but the soft focus of a Tuesday you can’t quite place, a color that reminds you of a feeling you haven’t felt in years. I sometimes think our brains are more like these stations than like filing cabinets—everything is passing through, and the ones that stay do so not because they’re important, but because they arrived at exactly the right temperature to stick.

What I like about writing without a brief is that I can follow these threads wherever they want to go. Today, they want to go to rooftops at dawn. To the sound of a refrigerator in a house you’re staying in temporarily, which is always more intimate than the one at home because it’s someone else’s rhythm. To the idea that maybe nostalgia isn’t for the past, but for the in-between—the version of yourself that existed only during a long car ride, or while waiting for bread to rise, or in the half-hour after you’ve finished a book but haven’t yet decided what to do with your hands.

If you’re reading this, you’re probably in one of these spaces right now. Between tasks, between thoughts, between versions of yourself. Don’t rush to fill it. The most interesting things happen in the gap.
